one_line: A short, single-run head-to-head of Cursor and Windsurf on a CLI task app, a web music player and pricing, with a verdict favoring Windsurf.
summary: The host compares Cursor and Windsurf after both shipped recent updates. Cursor moved its Composer UI from a separate window into the sidebar panel and added an early agent. Windsurf added image upload to Cascade, an explain-and-fix-problems feature, and a settings/instructions import from Cursor. The host runs two tests, each with one attempt per tool: a CLI task manager (add, list, delete tasks, tasks.json created) which both pass, and a web music player where Windsurf produces a simple HTML/JS/CSS page that plays an uploaded ElevenLabs voiceover while Cursor builds a larger app with a database that does not work until fixed. The host prefers Windsurf's scoping, then points to price: Windsurf Pro at $10 per month versus Cursor Pro at $20, plus a more generous free trial. The evidence is one anecdotal run per test with no repeats or metrics, and the pricing figures are as stated at recording time.

key_ideas.idea: Cursor moved its Composer from a separate window into the sidebar panel, and added an early agent mode.
key_ideas.detail: The host reads Cursor's changelog and guesses the sidebar move may be a response to Windsurf's Cascade sidebar. The rest of the changelog is described as smaller performance and fix items.

key_ideas.idea: Windsurf's Cascade gained image upload, so a sketch can be turned into a UI.
key_ideas.detail: The Windsurf team demo takes a napkin sketch of an 'Airbnb for dogs' landing page and generates it from a prompt. The host calls it a billion-dollar demo, which is marketing framing rather than evidence.

key_ideas.idea: Windsurf added a one-step import of Cursor settings and instructions.
key_ideas.detail: The host reads this as an explicit push to move Cursor users to Windsurf. He also notes Windsurf is weeks old, so the progress is impressive for its age.

key_ideas.idea: Test 1, a CLI task manager with explicit pass criteria, passes in both tools.
key_ideas.detail: The prompt asks for a task CLI and a pass means: it runs without errors, tasks can be added, and tasks.json is created. The host checks add, list and delete in each, and judges the test as measuring basic file read/write handling.

key_ideas.idea: Test 2, a full-stack web music player, separates the two tools.
key_ideas.detail: Windsurf builds a static HTML/JS/CSS player that plays an uploaded voiceover and has working volume control. Cursor builds a larger app with a database that does not play the song, and after a fix attempt the front end is still badly formatted. The host credits Windsurf for starting with a basic front end.

key_ideas.idea: On price, the host argues Windsurf is the better buy even if performance is equal.
key_ideas.detail: Both have a two-week trial. Cursor's trial allows 2,000 completions and 50 slow premium requests. Windsurf's free plan has unlimited auto-completions in the editor. The paid tiers are $10 for Windsurf and $20 for Cursor per month.

techniques.name: Same-prompt bake-off with explicit pass criteria
techniques.how: Send one identical prompt to each agent. Define the success check up front (runs without errors, feature X works, named output file exists). Run the result yourself and tick off each criterion. The host's CLI prompt covers add, list, delete, and checks tasks.json creation.
techniques.when: Comparing coding agents or IDE agents on a small greenfield task before choosing one. Use it as a cheap smoke test, since it exercises file read and write without needing a large setup.

techniques.name: Scope check with a deliberately simple app
techniques.how: Ask for a small web app with no obvious need for a database, such as a music player with an audio upload. Then check whether the agent picks a minimal stack or adds backend pieces that were not requested. Ask it how to start the app, then run it.
techniques.when: Measuring whether an agent over-engineers. In this video the Cursor run added a database that was not needed and then broke.

techniques.name: Trial and plan comparison before buying
techniques.how: Compare the free trial allowance (completions, premium/slow requests) and the paid monthly price side by side for each tool, and check whether the free tier alone covers the workload.
techniques.when: Choosing between paid AI IDEs for a team or personal use. Check current pricing directly, since the video's figures may have changed.

tools: ElevenLabs (voiceover audio used in the music-player test)
tasks.json (file created by the CLI test)

numbers.claim: Cursor free trial: 2,000 completions and 50 slow premium requests, two weeks.
Windsurf free plan has unlimited auto-completions in the editor. Both tools offer a two-week free trial.
Pro plan prices: Windsurf $10 per month, Cursor $20 per month (the host calls Windsurf half the price).

hot_takes: The host calls Windsurf's agent superior because it skipped a database for a simple music player. This rests on one run per tool, with no repeats.
Windsurf is 'significantly cheaper' and 'half the price' overall. This is pricing as stated at recording time, not checked against current plans.
The Windsurf sketch-to-landing-page demo is vendor material; the 'billion dollar business' line is a joke about the demo, not a result.
Hype title ('Before You CHOOSE') over a two-test, single-attempt comparison. The verdict is not supported by the sample size.

relevance.why: Editor-agent product comparison; no bearing on the proxy, memory, inference or sandbox stack.
ProsHarness wraps the Claude Code CLI, and this video only shows two single-run coding-agent smoke tests. Their pass criteria are a cheap check worth borrowing.
relevance.action: Reuse the CLI-task pass criteria (runs, add/list/delete work, output file created) as a quick acceptance check when comparing coding-agent runs.
